headline: High-risk shared-file and MCP interaction: ECC can write local state while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can write/read filesystem, use MCP, and stores prompts/skills/hooks in shared local paths; oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks. That creates a default pathway where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be parsed as instructions by the other. The pairwise interaction is documented only indirectly, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or config directory, prompt-like content can cross from one into the other.
IF either agent ingests file or MCP output as trusted instructions, injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate the two agents into distinct workspaces and config roots.
Disable MCPs for one side during cross-agent testing.
Add a manual review step before either agent executes instructions from files.
Use read-only mounts for shared reference material.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, security findings, and multiple local files; oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data, and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive material can flow from one agent into the other and then out via networked tools. The profiles do not prove isolation, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF the agents share any filesystem subtree, one can read the other's local artifacts.
IF either agent is given secrets or auth prompts in the shared workspace, those can be exposed in outputs or network calls.
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate home directory or container.
Remove secrets from shared folders before running either agent.
Restrict network egress on the agent handling sensitive files.
Rotate any credentials that were present in shared paths.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret isolation and audit logging.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and network egress; oh-my-openagent also has broad network egress and can spawn subprocesses. If both operate on the same repo or mutable workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces, so this is a default-dangerous conflict.
conditions: IF both agents are attached to the same git checkout, concurrent commits or edits can conflict.
IF either agent writes generated files into the other's working tree, overwrites are possible.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Disable git writes for one agent during shared tasks.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces session summaries, learned skills, and security findings; oh-my-openagent consumes project code and supports team/task messaging plus runtime MCPs. That makes it plausible for one agent's output to become the other's authoritative input, and then be acted on without verification. Because the pairwise handoff is not directly evidenced, uncertainty again favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF ECC-generated summaries or findings are fed into oh-my-openagent tasking, downstream actions can follow bad premises.
IF oh-my-openagent forwards unverified agent output into team_send_message or task creation, errors cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before task creation or messaging.
Mark inter-agent outputs as untrusted by default.
Add a verification checklist for facts and citations.
Limit one-way flow to summaries only, not instructions.
requires-engineering: implement confidence/provenance gating.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly touches security findings, git history, and multiple local config files; oh-my-openagent touches provider auth data, telemetry, and session history. The profiles suggest different retention and data-class handling, but they do not prove a residency or certification breach. The mismatch is plausible in default use, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated or customer data is stored in either agent's session history, retention mismatch can matter.
IF provider auth prompts or telemetry include personal data, compliance obligations may differ across the pair.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared sessions.
Review retention settings before use.
Disable telemetry where possible.
Separate customer-support data from developer tooling.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls per agent.
